A new group of adult participants (i.e., independent from the tracing accuracy experiment) based in the U.S. were recruited via Prolific for a 10-minute experiment, compensated at $12/hour, and asked to identify the category depicted in a subset of drawings.
Participants were shown these drawings in a random sequence and asked, "What category does this drawing belong to?".

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.text: The interaction between age (measured as a continuous variable) and drawing experience on recognizability is significant in the U.S. adult recognizability dataset (p = .008), but only marginally significant in the Kenya adult recognizability dataset (p = .056).

However, while there was a significant interaction between children's age and drawing experience on their drawing recognizability in the U.S. adult recognizability dataset, this interaction was only marginally significant in the Kenyan adult recognizability dataset (𝑏 = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.03,0.00], 𝑡(111) = -1.93, 𝑝 = .056).

Moreover, individual differences analyses found that younger children who drew more frequently in the past month produced more recognizable drawings than their counterparts who drew less frequently in the past month, though this result was only marginally significant in the Kenyan adult recognizability dataset.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > .22", "p > .40", "p-values > .33", 
"p's > .38", "p-values < .004", "p-values > .30", "p > .41"), 
    Text = c("All other variables were not significant (p > .22).", 
    "All other variables were not significant (p > .40).", "All other main effects and interactions were not significant (all p-values > .33).", 
    "Moreover, the output of the linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores (correctly or incorrectly identified) including fixed effects for child age and the aggregate homeitem factor and the interaction between the two showed a main effect of age (𝑏 = 0.11, 95% CI [0.10,0.13], 𝑡(116) = 13.32, 𝑝 < .001), but no other main effects or interactions (all p's > .38), suggesting that children's general home environments did not relate to their drawing recognizability scores.", 
    "In all four regressions, we found main effects of child age (all p-values < .004) and tracing ability (all pvalues < .001).", 
    "All other main effects and interactions were not significant (all p-values > .30).", 
    "All other variables were not significant (p > .41).")), row.names = c(NA, 
-7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .22", "p > .40", "p-values > .33", "p = .056", "p's > .38", "p-values > .30", "p > .41"), Sentence = c("All other variables were not significant (p > .22).", "All other variables were not significant (p > .40).", "All other main effects and interactions were not significant (all p-values > .33).", "The interaction between age (measured as a continuous variable) and drawing experience on recognizability is significant in the U.S. adult recognizability dataset (p = .008), but only marginally significant in the Kenya adult recognizability dataset (p = .056).", "Moreover, the output of the linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores (correctly or incorrectly identified) including fixed effects for child age and the aggregate homeitem factor and the interaction between the two showed a main effect of age (𝑏 = 0.11, 95% CI [0.10,0.13], 𝑡(116) = 13.32, 𝑝 < .001), but no other main effects or interactions (all p's > .38), suggesting that children's general home environments did not relate to their drawing recognizability scores.", "All other main effects and interactions were not significant (all p-values > .30).", "All other variables were not significant (p > .41).")), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. #### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2040 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (2040). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: were recruited via Prolific for a 10-minute experiment, compensated at $12/hour, and asked to rate the accuracy of a subset of tracings.
Participants were shown these tracings in a random sequence and asked to rate the quality of each tracing.
Additionally, 13 participants were excluded for missing the catch trial.

A new group of adult participants (i.e., independent from the tracing accuracy experiment) based in the U.S. were recruited via Prolific for a 10-minute experiment, compensated at $12/hour, and asked to identify the category depicted in a subset of drawings.
Participants were shown these drawings in a random sequence and asked, "What category does this drawing belong to?".

Although we initially preregistered collecting data from 144 participants, we ultimately collected data from 228 participants in order to ensure that each drawing was rated at least 10 times. 3 additional participants were excluded for answering incorrectly on the catch trial.
A new group of adult participants based in Kenya were recruited via BeSample for a 10minute experiment, compensated at $5/hour.
In addition to the 253 participants reported here, 80 additional participants were excluded for answering incorrectly on the catch trial.

Children were recruited from a local database maintained by a local non-profit organization, the Safe Water and AIDS Project (SWAP), and participated in the experiment in a quiet room at the SWAP office.
All parents of child participants provided informed consent.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it**, so before running it once more we copied it there: `Data and Analyses/full_recognition_data.csv` to `rebecca_data/full_recognition_data.csv` for `Kisumu Draw CogSci Analyses.Rmd`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.
**Calls that install packages in the code**

6 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. info.title: Developmental changes in children's production of line drawings in global contexts: Evidence from Kisumu, Kenya

text.text: Preregistration, materials, deidentified data, and analysis scripts for both experiments are publicly available at https://osf.io/wbmze.
text.formatted: Preregistration, materials, deidentified data, and analysis scripts for both experiments are publicly available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/wbmze">https://osf.io/wbmze</ref>.

text.text: Humans possess many powerful and flexible tools for communication, such as language, gesture, and graphical representation.

Drawing is a particularly important kind of communicative tool (Fan, Bainbridge, Chamberlain, & Wammes, 2023), given its early emergence in both ontogeny (Karmiloff-Smith, 1990; Sitton & Light, 1992) and phylogeny (Hoffmann et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Drawing is a particularly important kind of communicative tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fan, Bainbridge, Chamberlain, & Wammes, 2023)</ref>, given its early emergence in both ontogeny <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Karmiloff-Smith, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Sitton & Light, 1992)</ref> and phylogeny <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hoffmann et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In some cultures, at least, children draw from almost as soon as they can hold a crayon or marker.

Though early drawings are often rudimentary (Callaghan, 1999), some researchers have suggested that these early drawings can reflect meaningful features (e.g., shape, location, movement, animacy, size) even during young children's "scribbling stage" (Long et al., 2024; Matthews, 1984; 1998).
text.formatted: Though early drawings are often rudimentary <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Callaghan, 1999)</ref>, some researchers have suggested that these early drawings can reflect meaningful features (e.g., shape, location, movement, animacy, size) even during young children's "scribbling stage" <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Long et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Matthews, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">1998</ref>).

text.text: Children's drawings become substantially more recognizable with age continuously across two to ten years (Callaghan, 1999; Long, Fan, Huey, Chai, & Frank, 2024; Matthews, 1984).
text.formatted: Children's drawings become substantially more recognizable with age continuously across two to ten years <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Callaghan, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Long, Fan, Huey, Chai, & Frank, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Matthews, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: The features of children's drawings tend to change across age: younger children (e.g., 5-and 6-year-olds) draw what they have seen over time (e.g., a prototypical cup), whereas older children (e.g., 7-to 9-year-olds) draw what they see at a particular time (e.g., a specific cup placed in front of them at the time of drawing) (Barrett & Light, 1976; Bremner & Moore, 1984; Freeman & Janikoun, 1972).
text.formatted: The features of children's drawings tend to change across age: younger children (e.g., 5-and 6-year-olds) draw what they have seen over time (e.g., a prototypical cup), whereas older children (e.g., 7-to 9-year-olds) draw what they see at a particular time (e.g., a specific cup placed in front of them at the time of drawing) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barrett & Light, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bremner & Moore, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Freeman & Janikoun, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, pragmatic factors are important for drawing production: adults are sensitive to communicative contexts when producing drawings (Hawkins et al., 2023; Huey et al., 2023), and by approximately five or six years of age, children are also sensitive to communicative contexts when producing drawings (Light & McEwen, 1987;  CHILDREN'S PRODUCTION OF LINE DRAWINGS Sitton & Light, 1992).
text.formatted: Moreover, pragmatic factors are important for drawing production: adults are sensitive to communicative contexts when producing drawings <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hawkins et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Huey et al., 2023)</ref>, and by approximately five or six years of age, children are also sensitive to communicative contexts when producing drawings <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Light & McEwen, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> CHILDREN'S PRODUCTION OF LINE DRAWINGS <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Sitton & Light, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while children across many contexts produce drawings from an early age, multiple aspects of their drawings -such as drawing recognizability and the features of their drawings -improve or change with age.

Cross-culturally, US and Chinese children show similar developmental trajectories in their drawing production, specifically regarding the recognizability of their drawings (Long, Wang, Christie, Frank, & Fan, 2023).
text.formatted: Cross-culturally, US and Chinese children show similar developmental trajectories in their drawing production, specifically regarding the recognizability of their drawings <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Long, Wang, Christie, Frank, & Fan, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Though children in Beijing, China produced somewhat more recognizable drawings than children in San Jose, U.S.A., both groups showed age-related improvements in motor development (i.e., measured through a tracing task) and the recognizability of their drawings.

Notably, improvements in drawing production in both of these samples appeared to be driven by factors beyond simple motor development, perhaps due to changes in their internal representations of category information.
To date, quantitative evidence on drawing development comes from cultures in which visual media are ubiquitous and access to drawing materials is plentiful for children.
Less is known about the development of children's drawing production in early environments in which pictures, drawings, and other kinds of visual media are relatively less frequent.

While children growing up in high-income, urban contexts possess regular experience seeing and producing visual media, children in some low-income global contexts have relatively less access to visual media (Zhu, Kilonzo, Zhu, Fan, & Frank, 2026).
text.formatted: While children growing up in high-income, urban contexts possess regular experience seeing and producing visual media, children in some low-income global contexts have relatively less access to visual media <ref type="bibr">(Zhu, Kilonzo, Zhu, Fan, & Frank, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, some previous research suggests that children's early visual environments may influence their performance on picture-based tasks (Walker, Walker, & Ganea, 2013; Zhu, Kilonzo, Engelmann, & Gopnik, 2025).
text.formatted: Indeed, some previous research suggests that children's early visual environments may influence their performance on picture-based tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Walker, Walker, & Ganea, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhu, Kilonzo, Engelmann, & Gopnik, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: How do children's early visual environments influence their drawing production trajectories?

One possibility is that children's drawing production trajectories strongly depend on their visual media experiences (i.e., experiences viewing visual media, such as picture books, televisions, tablets), drawing experiences (i.e., experiences creating drawings), or both.

In early environments with relatively frequent access to visual media and drawing opportunities (e.g., San Jose, U.S.A.; Beijing, China), children may show age-related improvements in drawing production because their early play activities often involve visual representations (e.g., drawing, reading picture books, watching television).

In contrast, in early environments with relatively infrequent access to drawing opportunities (e.g., Kisumu, Kenya, our focus here), children may not show the same age-related improvements in drawing production because their early play activities (e.g., running, soccer) often involve both less visual media and drawing opportunities.
On this account, while basic motoric development might lead to some age-related improvements, they would be expected to be relatively minimal after controlling for these factors.
However, another possibility is that children's drawing production trajectories do not depend, or only weakly depend, on their visual media experiences and drawing opportunities.

Children may develop an increasingly mature capacity to draw with little, if any, visual media experience or drawing experience; rather, age-related improvements in drawing production may be related to children's increasing conceptual knowledge and visual recognition abilities (Bova et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Children may develop an increasingly mature capacity to draw with little, if any, visual media experience or drawing experience; rather, age-related improvements in drawing production may be related to children's increasing conceptual knowledge and visual recognition abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bova et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: To explore whether early visual environments influence children's drawing production trajectories, we work with children growing up in Kisumu, Kenya, an environment with relatively less visual media compared to urban and suburban Western convenience sample environments.
Kisumu is the third largest city in Kenya, and a small metro region containing a population of approximately one million individuals.
The majority of Kisumu households are classified as low or middle socioeconomic status, with substantial variation in income levels and access to basic household assets (Were et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The majority of Kisumu households are classified as low or middle socioeconomic status, with substantial variation in income levels and access to basic household assets <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Were et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Kisumu children possess substantial amounts of variation in their early experiences with visual media (Zhu, Pitchik, et al., 2025; Zhu, Kilonzo, et al., 2026), and low-to-middle-income Kisumu children's early environments typically involve less visual media (i.e., drawing materials, picture books) than high-income American children's early environments (Zhu, Martinez-Krams, Arieda, Kilonzo, Fan, & Frank, 2026).
text.formatted: Kisumu children possess substantial amounts of variation in their early experiences with visual media <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Zhu, Pitchik, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Zhu, Kilonzo, et al., 2026)</ref>, and low-to-middle-income Kisumu children's early environments typically involve less visual media (i.e., drawing materials, picture books) than high-income American children's early environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Zhu, Martinez-Krams, Arieda, Kilonzo, Fan, & Frank, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For example, in previous research, caregivers of low-to-middle-income Kisumu children reported an average of approximately three picture books, ten drawing materials (i.e., pens, pencils, crayons, markers), three posters, and six toys in their homes, whereas caregivers of high-income San Francisco Bay Area children reported an average of approximately 111 picture books, 56 drawing materials, 19 posters, and 104 toys in their homes (Zhu, Martinez-Krams, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, in previous research, caregivers of low-to-middle-income Kisumu children reported an average of approximately three picture books, ten drawing materials (i.e., pens, pencils, crayons, markers), three posters, and six toys in their homes, whereas caregivers of high-income San Francisco Bay Area children reported an average of approximately 111 picture books, 56 drawing materials, 19 posters, and 104 toys in their homes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Zhu, Martinez-Krams, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While visual media experiences vary, the vast majority of Kisumu children do receive some amount of drawing experience through their formal schooling experiences.
Kisumu children typically begin preschool between 3-4 years of age, though in Kenya, there can be some variation in age at the start of formal schooling.

For example, previous research involving children just in their first month of formal schooling (i.e., pre-primary 1) in Mombasa County, Kenya, lists an age range from 2-7 years (Zhu, Kilonzo, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, previous research involving children just in their first month of formal schooling (i.e., pre-primary 1) in Mombasa County, Kenya, lists an age range from 2-7 years <ref type="bibr">(Zhu, Kilonzo, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: One co-author (JOA), who is both a member of the Kisumu community and the parent of young children growing up in Kisumu, noted that Kisumu daycares and preschools emphasize the importance of drawing as part of the curriculum, and typically require parents to provide basic drawing materials as part of the child's enrollment requirements.

Moreover, Kenya's education system has recently encouraged increased parental involvement in early learning activities, prompting more parents to participate in and supervise drawing activities of their preschool-and elementary-aged children.
Kisumu children begin drawing in their first year of preschool (i.e., pre-primary 1) in an unstructured manner, for example by drawing or scribbling anything, or coloring.
During their second year of preschool (i.e., pre-primary 2), Kisumu children are introduced to more specific tasks, such as tracing, connecting dots, or drawing specific animals or shapes.
Despite these factors, there is still substantial variation in children's early drawing experiences, particularly at the household level.
In resource-constrained households, in which families may have limited financial access to store-bought drawing materials, children often draw using sticks in soil.
In contrast, Kisumu families with greater economic means often provide children with writing and drawing tools (i.e., pencils, pens, crayons, paper).
If left unsupervised, children might also draw on household walls and floors.
Thus, Kisumu children have substantial variation in access to, and experience with, drawing materials in their homes.

The present study seeks to leverage this within-context variation to conduct individual differences analyses, asking whether children's individual drawing experiences might influence their drawing production.

By investigating variation within a single context rather than across contexts, we avoid potential confounders such as linguistic or pragmatic differences that are likely to vary across countries (Bohn, Fong, Pope-Caldwell, Stengelin, & Haun, 2024; Draper et al., 2022).
text.formatted: By investigating variation within a single context rather than across contexts, we avoid potential confounders such as linguistic or pragmatic differences that are likely to vary across countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bohn, Fong, Pope-Caldwell, Stengelin, & Haun, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Draper et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, in the present research we ask: at a group level, does drawing recognizability increase with age in Kisumu, a context with relatively less visual media compared to urban and suburban Western convenience sample contexts, independent of developmental improvements in motor control?
Moreover, at an individual level, does drawing recognizability increase with children's drawing experiences, independent of developmental improvements in motor control?
Children completed a one-on-one drawing session under the supervision of a local experimenter in their native language, Swahili.
On each trial, children were provided with a 8.5x11 sheet of paper, and drew on the paper using a blue Crayola marker.
On the tracing trials, the shape to be traced was printed in light gray on the paper.
On the drawing trials, the paper was blank.
The experimenter first demonstrated the task to the child by tracing a vertical line on a sheet of paper.

After watching the experimenter demonstration, children completed five tracing trials in a fixed order of increasing difficulty (i.e., horizontal line, triangle, circle, circular shape, angular shape; see Fig 1), thus providing a baseline measure of visuomotor control.

text.text: After the tracing trials, children were asked to draw 12 object categories in a random order ("airplane" / "ndege ya kubeba watu", "bicycle" / "baiskeli", "bird" / "ndege mnyama", "car"/ "gari", "cat" / "paka", "chair" / "kiti", "cup" / "kikombe", "hat" / "kofia", "house"/ "nyumba", "rabbit" / "sungura", "tree" / "mti", "watch" / "saa"; see Fig 2).

text.text: In order to investigate how individual children's experiences and home environments might relate to their drawing abilities, each child's caregiver completed a brief questionnaire through a 15-minute in-person interview with a local researcher.

Caregivers provided additional information regarding children's experiences with drawing (e.g., "In the past month, how often did your child draw using pens, pencils, crayons, or markers?") as well as other caregiver and home environment variables such as frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education.

These questions were adapted from a CHILDREN'S PRODUCTION OF LINE DRAWINGS previous caregiver questionnaire used in Kisumu and Mombasa (Zhu, Pitchik, et al., 2025; Zhu, Kilonzo, Engelmann, et al., 2025), as well as a standardized demographic reporting tool meant for use across cultures (Singh et al., 2024).

text.text: Since income level is a sensitive topic in this community, we measure socioeconomic status through maternal education levels, a methodological choice that is consistent with both previous research in Kenyan contexts (Zhu, Kilonzo, et al., 2025; Zhu, Pitchik et al., 2025) and broader recommendations for measuring socioeconomic status (Antonoplis, 2023).

We measured children's tracing accuracy by gathering ratings of their tracings via an online experiment in which adults provided empirical judgments.
Adult participants based in the U.S.
were recruited via Prolific for a 10-minute experiment, compensated at $12/hour, and asked to rate the accuracy of a subset of tracings.
Each participant saw two tracings from each of the six one-year age bins and five tracing types, thus leading each participant to view 60 tracings in total.
Participants were shown these tracings in a random sequence and asked to rate the quality of each tracing.
Participants selected a single response from a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very bad,2 = bad,3 = neither good nor bad,4 = good,5 = very good).

A catch trial (i.e., a triangle shape to be traced, with blue marker scribbles inside the triangle) was included to verify that participants could accurately identify an unambiguously bad tracing (i.e., by rating the bad tracing as either bad or very bad).
The sample size was not preregistered.
We collected data from 124 participants in order to ensure that each tracing was rated at least 10 times.
Additionally, 13 participants were excluded for missing the catch trial.
For each child, we averaged each tracing type's ratings, generating five tracing averages per child.
We then averaged these averages to create a single tracing score for each child.

Since some tracings might be easier than other tracings (i.e., it may be easier to trace a straight line than a complicated curved shape), this ensured that each tracing was given the same weight in the final score.
Following previous studies exploring children's drawing recognizability (Long et al., 2023), we measured the recognizability of each drawing via an online, 12-AFC categorization experiment.
text.formatted: Following previous studies exploring children's drawing recognizability <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Long et al., 2023)</ref>, we measured the recognizability of each drawing via an online, 12-AFC categorization experiment.

text.text: A new group of adult participants (i.e., independent from the tracing accuracy experiment) based in the U.S. were recruited via Prolific for a 10-minute experiment, compensated at $12/hour, and asked to identify the category depicted in a subset of drawings.
Each participant saw one drawing from each of the six one-year age bins and twelve categories, thus leading each participant to view 72 drawings in total.
Participants were shown these drawings in a random sequence and asked, "What category does this drawing belong to?".
Participants selected a single response from the set of 12 categories.

A catch trial (i.e., a clearly identifiable drawing of a plane) was included to verify that participants could accurately recognize an unambiguous drawing (i.e., by selecting the "plane" response category).

Although we initially preregistered collecting data from 144 participants, we ultimately collected data from 228 participants in order to ensure that each drawing was rated at least 10 times. 3 additional participants were excluded for answering incorrectly on the catch trial.

It is possible that Kisumu children's drawings may be more recognizable to adults living in a similar environment (i.e., Kenya) rather than adults living in a markedly different environment (i.e., the U.S.).
Thus, we also ran the same drawing recognizability experiment with Kenyan adults.
A new group of adult participants based in Kenya were recruited via BeSample for a 10minute experiment, compensated at $5/hour.

The Kenyan adult drawing recognizability experiment was identical to the U.S. adult drawing recognizability experiment (e.g., each participant saw one drawing from each of the six one-year age bins and twelve categories, participated in English, and completed one attention check).
Although we initially preregistered collecting data from 144 participants, we ultimately collected data from 253 participants in order to ensure that each drawing was rated at least 10 times.
In addition to the 253 participants reported here, 80 additional participants were excluded for answering incorrectly on the catch trial.
While it is unclear why a notable proportion of Kenyan adults failed the attention check, we speculate that it was due in part to participants' poor Internet connections.
Six Kenyan adult participants emailed to let us know that the pictures in the survey were not loading, whereas no U.S. adult participants contacted us about this error.
Moreover, Kenyan adult participants did not contact us with any other kinds of concerns or errors.
Our first research question concerned developmental differences in drawing recognizability.

We fit a preregistered generalized linear mixed-effects model to U.S. adult recognizability scores (correctly or incorrectly identified), including a fixed effect for child age, a random slope for the effect of age on each object category, and a random intercept for each child.
Drawing recognizability increased with age (𝛽 ̂= 0.75, 95% CI [0.60,0.90], 𝑧 = 9.55, 𝑝 < .001).

text.text: We next ran an analysis controlling for children's tracing abilities.

An exploratory mixedeffects model was fit to drawing recognizability scores (correctly or incorrectly identified), including fixed effects for child age and tracing abilities, a random slope for the effect of age on each object category, and a random intercept for each child.

This model showed main effects of age (𝛽 ̂= 0.37, 95% CI [0.19,0.55], 𝑧 = 3.98, 𝑝 < .001) and tracing ability (𝛽 ̂= 1.00, 95% CI [0.70,1.30], 𝑧 = 6.53, 𝑝 < .001) on drawing recognizability (see Fig. 3).

To explore whether drawing recognizability was positively related to children's drawing experiences, an exploratory linear regression was fit to each child's aggregate drawing recognizability score, investigating effects of drawing frequency and age and the interaction CHILDREN'S PRODUCTION OF LINE DRAWINGS between the two variables, with covariates for tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education.

We found main effects of child age (𝑏 = 0.05, 95% CI [0.02,0.07], 𝑡(111) = 4.21, 𝑝 < .001) and tracing ability (𝑏 = 0.17, 95% CI [0.12,0.21], 𝑡(111) = 7.47, 𝑝 < .001), and an interaction between drawing frequency and age (𝑏 = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.04, -0.01], 𝑡(111) = -2.69, 𝑝 = .008), such that the positive relation between drawing frequency and drawing recognizability was stronger for younger children (see Fig. 5).

text.text: Moreover, we compared the full drawing experience model to two simpler models.

The full drawing experience model was a linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores, including effects of child age and drawing frequency and the interaction between the two, with covariates for tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education.

The first simpler model, without a child age and drawing frequency interaction term, was a linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores, including effects of child age and drawing frequency, with covariates for tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education.

The second simpler model, which did not include drawing frequency at all, was a linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores, including effects of child age, tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education.

The full model fit the data better than both the first simpler model, adjusted R-squared = .74 and .73 respectively, F(1, 111) = 7.25, p = .01, and the second simpler model, adjusted R-squared = .74 and .73 respectively, F(2, 111) = 3.98, p = .02).

Thus, drawing CHILDREN'S PRODUCTION OF LINE DRAWINGS experience, child age, and the interaction between the two are important variables when accounting for individual variation in children's drawing recognizability.

To determine whether drawing recognizability was related specifically to children's drawing experiences, as opposed to children's general home environments, we also explored whether drawing recognizability related to any of the control variables and their age interactions.

To explore the role of tracing ability, an exploratory linear regression was fit to each child's aggregate drawing recognizability score, investigating fixed effects for tracing ability and age and the interaction between the two variables, controlling for drawing frequency, frequency of childdirected speech, frequency of play, number of toys, and maternal education.

We found main effects of child age (𝑏 = 0.06, 95% CI [0.03,0.08], 𝑡(111) = 4.94, 𝑝 < .001) and tracing ability (𝑏 = 0.13, 95% CI [0.07,0.18], 𝑡(111) = 4.59, 𝑝 < .001), and an interaction between tracing ability and age (𝑏 = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.05, -0.01], 𝑡(111) = -2.74, 𝑝 = .007), such that the positive relation between tracing ability and drawing recognizability was stronger for younger children.

text.text: Finally, we ran the same analyses, but fit to Kenyan adult recognizability scores rather than U.S. adult recognizability scores.

Results from the analyses involving U.S. adult recognizability ratings and the analyses involving Kenyan adult recognizability ratings were largely identical (see Appendix B for full Kenyan adult recognizability score results).
In both the U.S. adult and Kenyan adult recognizability datasets, children's drawing recognizability increased with age and tracing ability.

However, while there was a significant interaction between children's age and drawing experience on their drawing recognizability in the U.S. adult recognizability dataset, this interaction was only marginally significant in the Kenyan adult recognizability dataset (𝑏 = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.03,0.00], 𝑡(111) = -1.93, 𝑝 = .056).
How does drawing ability develop in cultures with more variable visual media exposure and drawing experiences in early childhood?

We found steady age-related improvement in the recognizability of drawings from 4-to 9-year-olds growing up in Kisumu, Kenya, an environment with relatively less visual media compared to urban and suburban Western convenience sample environments.
Similar to prior work, we also found that children's developing visuomotor abilities do not account for all of the developmental change in their drawing abilities.
Moreover, these age-related results were robust across two separate datasets, one involving recognizability ratings from U.S. adults and another involving recognizability ratings from Kenyan adults.

Thus, low-to-middle-income Kisumu children growing up in an environment with relatively less access to drawing materials show a similar age-related developmental trajectory to middle-to-high-income children from U.S. and Chinese convenience samples growing up in environments with relatively more access to drawing materials (Long et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Thus, low-to-middle-income Kisumu children growing up in an environment with relatively less access to drawing materials show a similar age-related developmental trajectory to middle-to-high-income children from U.S. and Chinese convenience samples growing up in environments with relatively more access to drawing materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Long et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In Kisumu, Beijing, and San Jose, 8-and 9-year-olds produced the most recognizable drawings, while younger children's drawings were less recognizable.

Moreover, individual differences analyses found that younger children who drew more frequently in the past month produced more recognizable drawings than their counterparts who drew less frequently in the past month, though this result was only marginally significant in the Kenyan adult recognizability dataset.

Thus, while the overall dataset suggests similar age-related developmental trajectories in three contexts despite contextual variations in drawing opportunities and visual media experience, the finding that younger children's drawing experiences positively relate to their drawing production shows that some minor amount of drawing experience is likely still necessary for the development of drawing production when the capacity first emerges in ontogenesis.

By investigating variation in drawing experience and drawing recognizability within a single early childhood context, we avoid potential confounding by differences such as translation of task instructions and language spoken in the home, which are more likely to differ across geographically diverse contexts (Bohn et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By investigating variation in drawing experience and drawing recognizability within a single early childhood context, we avoid potential confounding by differences such as translation of task instructions and language spoken in the home, which are more likely to differ across geographically diverse contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bohn et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, by isolating the effects of specific variables (i.e., drawing experience) from broader effects of culture and context, we might expect the present findings (i.e., the possible relation between drawing experience and production) to be more likely generalize to children growing up in other diverse cultures and contexts.
However, more empirical research is necessary to definitively investigate the generalizability of the present findings.

Moreover, the present research also explored the effects of not only drawing experience (e.g., experiences drawing with pens, pencils, markers), but also overall home environment (e.g., number of toys, drawing materials, picture books, and posters in the home) on children's drawing production.

The present results suggest a specific link between drawing experience and drawing production, independent of other home environment factors, such as overall presence of visual representations and toys in the home.
Consequently, the present research suggests that, for younger children, direct experiences with creating drawings, rather than experience viewing visual media, improve drawing abilities.

However, future research should investigate the relation between drawing production and other kinds of visual media experience (e.g., playing with tablets), which were not measured in the present research.

While the present research finds a positive relation between drawing experience on drawing production, it is possible that overall visual media experience is also positively related to children's developing drawing production abilities.
Our work has some limitations.

For example, we made the methodological choice to use the same object categories as previous drawing studies (Long et al., 2023), in order to better license future cross-contextual comparisons (Cohn, 2014; Du et al., 2026; Restoy et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, we made the methodological choice to use the same object categories as previous drawing studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Long et al., 2023)</ref>, in order to better license future cross-contextual comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohn, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Du et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Restoy et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While the majority of the categories were appropriate for Kisumu children, we note that some categories might be less appropriate.
For example, local collaborators noted that rabbits are uncommon in Kisumu, and children's rabbit drawings were indeed less recognizable than their other drawings (see Fig. 4).
text.formatted: For example, local collaborators noted that rabbits are uncommon in Kisumu, and children's rabbit drawings were indeed less recognizable than their other drawings (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: Thus, we caution against using the present data as an absolute measure of Kisumu children's drawing production abilities, as children would likely have produced more recognizable drawings if prompted with more familiar categories.

Due to methodological differences between the present study (i.e., conducted using marker and paper, using a category which is less familiar) and previous research with U.S. and Chinese children (i.e., conducted using tablets, using only familiar categories), we note that the present data are not useful for comparisons of overall performance across contexts (Frank et al., 2024), but rather are useful for examining whether the same broad patterns of performance emerge in multiple contexts.
text.formatted: Due to methodological differences between the present study (i.e., conducted using marker and paper, using a category which is less familiar) and previous research with U.S. and Chinese children (i.e., conducted using tablets, using only familiar categories), we note that the present data are not useful for comparisons of overall performance across contexts <ref type="bibr">(Frank et al., 2024)</ref>, but rather are useful for examining whether the same broad patterns of performance emerge in multiple contexts.

text.text: Nonetheless, the familiarity, or lack thereof, of a category may lead to interesting future research questions: for example, what might children draw if asked to draw broad superordinate categories, such as animals or objects?
Future research might investigate how world knowledge, as well as drawing experience, affects children's drawing production.

Moreover, while the present research establishes a correlational link between children's drawing experience and the recognizability of their drawings, future research might better establish a more direct causal link between the two variables through experimental training studies or, at a minimum, longitudinal designs.

Future research might also consider including longer caregiver questionnaires with more detailed measures of children's home environments and experiences (e.g., including measures of various kinds of play, paternal education in addition to maternal education).

Overall, the present findings show that Kisumu, Kenya children growing up in an environment with less visual media relative to urban and suburban Western convenience sample environments show age-related improvements in their drawing production.
This developmental trajectory is remarkably similar to San Jose, U.S. children and Beijing, China children growing up in different (i.e., relatively picture-frequent) contexts (Long et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This developmental trajectory is remarkably similar to San Jose, U.S. children and Beijing, China children growing up in different (i.e., relatively picture-frequent) contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Long et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, we leverage the large degree of within-context variation in Kisumu to show that drawing experience is positively related to drawing recognizability for young children.
These findings provide insight into how children worldwide become competent communicators of visual information.

To investigate developmental differences in drawing recognizability, we fit a preregistered mixed-effects model to drawing Kenyan adult recognizability scores (correctly or incorrectly identified), including a fixed effect for child age, a random slope for the effect of age on each object category, and a random intercept for each child.

text.text: We next ran an analysis controlling for children's tracing abilities.

A preregistered mixedeffects model was fit to drawing recognizability scores (correctly or incorrectly identified), including fixed effects for child age and tracing abilities, a random slope for the effect of age on each object category, and a random intercept for each child.
This model showed main effects of age (𝛽 ̂= 0.17, 95% CI [0.05,0.28], 𝑧 = 2.90, 𝑝 = .004) and tracing ability (𝛽 ̂= 0.97, 95% CI [0.74,1.20], 𝑧 = 8.32, 𝑝 < .001) on drawing recognizability.

To explore the role of tracing ability, an exploratory linear regression was fit to each child's aggregate drawing recognizability score, investigating fixed effects for tracing ability and age and the interaction between the two variables, controlling for drawing frequency, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys, and maternal education.

We found main effects of child age For all other home environment variables, exploratory linear regressions were fit to each child's aggregate drawing recognizability score, investigating fixed effects for the home environment variable (e.g., child-directed speech) and age and the interaction between the two variables, controlling for the other home environment variables (e.g., play, toys, maternal education).
Thus, we conducted four exploratory linear regressions, one for each home environment variable (i.e., child-directed speech, play, toys, maternal education).
In all four regressions, we found main effects of child age (all p-values < .004) and tracing ability (all pvalues < .001).

Participants.A preregistered sample of 120 4-to 9-year-olds (M = 6.96 years, SD = 1.70 years, range = 4.01 -9.89 years, 58 girls, 62 boys, 20 children in each 1-year age bin) growing up in Kisumu, Kenya participated.
All children in the sample, except for one 4-year-old, were already attending daycare or school.

Researchers tested three additional 5-year-olds, whose data was excluded due to experimenter error (two children) and a failure to comply with the instructions (one child who only wrote alphabet letters, rather than drawing).

Children were recruited from a local database maintained by a local non-profit organization, the Safe Water and AIDS Project (SWAP), and participated in the experiment in a quiet room at the SWAP office.

The experiment was approved by a U.S. university's Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects, as well as by the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI), the National Commission for Science, Technology, and Innovation (NACOSTI), and the local Kisumu County government.
All parents of child participants provided informed consent.
All data were collected in August and September 2024.

All other variables were not significant (p > .35). For full regression results, see Table 2. Moreover, we compared the full drawing experience model to two simpler models. The full drawing experience model was a linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores, including effects of child age and drawing frequency and the interaction between the two, with covariates for tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education. The first simpler model, without a child age and drawing frequency interaction term, was a linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores, including effects of child age and drawing frequency, with covariates for tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education. The second simpler model, which did not include drawing frequency at all, was a linear regression fit to drawing recognizability scores, including effects of child age, tracing ability, frequency of child-directed speech, frequency of play, number of toys in the home, and maternal education. The full model did not fit the data better than either the first simpler model, adjusted R-squared = .73 and .72 respectively, F(1, 111) = 3.73, p = .06, or the second simpler model, adjusted R-squared = .73 and .73 respectively, F(2, 111) = 2.32, p = .10).
